create a python project following the instruction and create the ENV by using UV: "Human-in-the-Loop (Interactive) Model Training

You can implement an interactive, human-in-the-loop training loop where a base model makes predictions, a user corrects them, and those corrections are used to update the model. In practice this means: train an initial model on your data; use it to label new examples; present predictions in a GUI; let the user add missing labels or remove false positives; then incorporate those corrected examples into the training set and re-train (or fine-tune) the model. As CVAT’s documentation explains, “a small, manually labeled dataset…is used to train an initial model. Once trained, the model begins labeling new, unlabeled data. These labels are then reviewed by human annotators… The corrections made by humans are then given back to the model and…used to refine and improve it further”
cvat.ai
. Repeating this cycle gradually improves accuracy over time.

Key steps in this interactive loop are:

Initial Training: Train a model on whatever labeled data you have.

Predict & Annotate: Use the model to predict on new images/text/rows. In a GUI (see below), show these predictions (e.g. bounding boxes on images).

User Correction: The user corrects errors – draws missing boxes, erases incorrect boxes, fixes segmentation masks, corrects text labels, etc. These edits become new ground-truth labels.

Data Update: Save the corrected labels and merge them into your training set.

Retrain/Update Model: After enough new examples (the “buffer”), update the model. This can be done via incremental learning (partial updates) or by fine-tuning on the expanded dataset.

Iterate: Go back to “Predict” with the improved model and repeat.

This hybrid (automated+human) annotation process (also called active learning or incremental learning) leverages automation for routine labeling while human effort focuses on correcting mistakes
cvat.ai
. Over time, as the model improves, fewer corrections are needed and the model can label more data automatically.

Tools & Interfaces

You’ll need a labeling interface that displays model predictions and accepts user edits. Fortunately, several open-source tools and frameworks support this:

CVAT (Computer Vision Annotation Tool) – a web-based open-source tool for images/video. It lets you integrate custom models (e.g. YOLO for detection or a segmentation CNN) so that it auto-generates annotations which you then correct. For example, CVAT can wrap models (like YOLOvX or Meta’s Segment Anything Model) as plug-ins: “models (e.g., YOLOv11 or SAM2) are wrapped as Nuclio functions…once deployed, models are added to CVAT’s model registry for use in auto-annotation”
cvat.ai
. In the CVAT GUI you then review and correct these auto-annotations (bounding boxes, polygons, masks, etc.) before exporting the final labels.

Label Studio – a versatile, browser-based annotation platform supporting images, text, audio, and more. It allows you to set up tasks (e.g. bounding boxes on images, polygons, or text classification spans) with a user-friendly UI. Label Studio also has an ML backend feature: you can plug in your own model (even YOLO or a CNN) to pre-label the data, then let annotators fix it
github.com
. After corrections, you can export the updated annotations for retraining.

Doccano – an open-source text annotation tool. For NLP tasks (text classification, entity labeling, sequence labeling, etc.), Doccano provides a web UI to label text samples
github.com
. You could use it to display model-predicted labels for text and let the user adjust them.

Custom GUIs (Streamlit, Gradio, etc.) – If you need a more tailored or lightweight solution, Python frameworks like Streamlit or Gradio let you quickly build web apps. For example, you can display an image with boxes overlayed, and use drawing widgets (Streamlit’s image annotation component or Gradio’s interactive tools) to allow corrections. Similarly, for tabular data you could make a simple form to show model predictions for each row and let the user change them.

In summary, use annotation tools (CVAT, Label Studio, Doccano, etc.) for standard workflows. They support exporting in formats (e.g. COCO, YOLO, CSV) that you can feed back into training. Label Studio is advertised as “a multi-type data labeling and annotation tool” for images, text, audio, and more
github.com
. These GUIs handle the manual steps, while you handle the model training pipeline behind the scenes.

Incremental Training / Updating

The core of the system is how to update the model with new labels. Two main approaches are used:

Incremental (Online) Learning: Some algorithms support updating on-the-fly via methods like scikit-learn’s partial_fit. If your task is, say, text classification or simple regression, models like SGDClassifier, Perceptron, PassiveAggressive, or Naive Bayes can incrementally incorporate new examples without retraining from scratch. As scikit-learn docs note, “all estimators implementing the partial_fit API are candidates” for incremental learning, allowing you to feed mini-batches of new data to continually update the model
scikit-learn.org
. For example, if a user corrects the label of a sentence or adds a new data row, you could call model.partial_fit(new_features, new_labels, classes=...). This immediately updates the model weights based on just that example (or small batch). Using partial_fit avoids having to reload the entire dataset each time.

Batch Fine-Tuning: For neural networks (CNNs for images, YOLO detectors, segmentation models, etc.), you typically perform fine-tuning on the augmented dataset. That is, append the new (corrected) labeled samples to your dataset and continue training from the last checkpoint. In practice, this often means calling your training script again with the same model (loading previous weights) on the extended data. For instance, Ultralytics YOLO lets you resume training seamlessly: setting resume=True causes it to load the last .pt checkpoint (including optimizer state) and continue training
docs.ultralytics.com
. So after collecting new image annotations, you could run: model = YOLO('best.pt'); model.train(data='updated_data.yaml', epochs=10, resume=True), which fine-tunes the existing detector on the new examples. This effectively incrementally teaches the model the user’s corrections without starting from scratch. The Ultralytics docs explicitly state: “By setting resume=True, the train function will continue training from where it left off, using the state stored in the last saved model
docs.ultralytics.com
.”

For segmentation models (e.g. Mask R-CNN or U-Net), the logic is analogous: treat user-corrected masks as new ground truth, add them to your training data, and continue training. Every few corrections or epochs, you can re-evaluate the model to see improved segmentation. Even if your framework doesn’t support exact incremental updates, you can always fine-tune by training a few more epochs on the combination of old and new data.

Generic Workflow (All Data Types)

Putting it all together, a generic pipeline looks like this:

Initial Model: Train a model on your initial labeled dataset (images/text/tabular).

Automated Labeling: Use this model to predict on new unlabeled or previously labeled data.

User Review in GUI: Show the predictions to the user in a GUI (CVAT/LabelStudio for images, Doccano or custom UI for text, a simple table/UI for tabular data). The user corrects the labels (adds/removes boxes or fixes classes).

Collect Corrections: Save these corrected labels (e.g. export CSV/JSON from the tool).

Buffering: Once you have accumulated a batch of new labels (e.g. 50–100 examples or whenever convenient), proceed to update the model.

Model Update: Depending on your approach:

If using partial updates: call model.partial_fit(...) (scikit-learn) or apply an online update for each new sample
scikit-learn.org
.

If fine-tuning: combine the new examples with your existing training set and continue training (e.g. using resume=True in YOLO
docs.ultralytics.com
 or additional epochs in your DL framework).

Repeat: Use the updated model for the next round of predictions. Continue iterating this predict-review-update loop.

Over time, the model learns from the user’s corrections. The CVAT blog describes this hybrid approach: “Once trained, the model begins labeling new… data. These labels are then reviewed by human annotators… The corrections made by humans are then given back to the model… As the cycle repeats, the model becomes increasingly accurate and reliable”
cvat.ai
. This strategy works for images (detection/segmentation), text (classification/NER), and tabular data alike.

Data-Type Notes

Object Detection (YOLO, etc.): Use an annotation tool like CVAT or Label Studio to display image detections. The user can draw bounding boxes or delete wrong ones. After collecting corrected boxes (in YOLO format or COCO JSON), fine-tune your detector by continuing training. YOLO’s framework makes this easy via its resume training option
docs.ultralytics.com
.

Image Segmentation (CNN): Similar to detection, except the user edits segmentation masks (polygons or bitmasks) in the GUI. You’ll want a tool that supports mask/polygon editing (CVAT can handle masks). Then continue training your segmentation model (U-Net, Mask R-CNN, etc.) on the corrected masks. New training can incorporate these masks to improve accuracy on subtle edges.

Text Classification/NER: Use a web-based text-labeling UI (Doccano
github.com
, Label Studio, or a custom form) to show model-predicted labels on each sentence or document. The user corrects labels or entity spans. Then update your classifier (e.g. using scikit-learn’s partial_fit on the new examples
scikit-learn.org
, or fine-tune a transformer model on all data).

Tabular Data: Present data rows and the model’s prediction (class or value) in a simple GUI or spreadsheet-like interface. The user corrects any wrong labels or values. You can then call partial_fit on these rows (if using online learners) or re-run training on the growing dataset.

Throughout, try to automate as much as possible: for example, write a script that listens for completed annotation tasks (exports) and automatically triggers the retraining step when new labels are added. Many annotation platforms have APIs or command-line tools to fetch labels, so you can integrate training pipelines (for instance, CVAT has a CLI to download annotations, and Label Studio can be scripted or has a REST API).

Summary

In summary, the easiest way to build an adaptive model is via a human-in-the-loop cycle: use a model to auto-annotate, let the user correct those annotations in a GUI (such as CVAT, Label Studio, or a custom web app), and then re-train the model on the corrected data. Incremental-learning techniques (e.g. scikit-learn’s partial_fit
scikit-learn.org
 or YOLO’s resume training
docs.ultralytics.com
) make the updates efficient. Over multiple rounds, this hybrid approach yields a model that continuously improves with each batch of user feedback
cvat.ai
.

Sources: This answer combines general best practices for active/human-in-loop learning with documented features of tools (e.g. CVAT/CVAT blog on HITL
cvat.ai
 and YOLO’s training docs
docs.ultralytics.com
) and knowledge of incremental learning in Python (scikit-learn partial_fit
scikit-learn.org
, Label Studio/Doccano capabilities
github.com
github.com
).

# Define supported extensions as a global constant
SUPPORTED_EXTENSIONS = (".png", ".jpg", ".jpeg")


class AnnotationTool:
    def __init__(
        self, master, image_dir="images", annotation_dir="dataset", crop_dir="crops"
    ):
        self.master = master
        self.image_dir = image_dir
        self.annotation_dir = annotation_dir
        self.crop_dir = crop_dir

        self.label_file = os.path.join(self.annotation_dir, "labels.json")
        self.labels_all_dir = os.path.join(self.annotation_dir, "labels_all")

        os.makedirs(self.annotation_dir, exist_ok=True)

        self.image_ids = sorted(
            [
                f

        )
        self.index = 0
        self.image_ext_map = {

            if f.lower().endswith(SUPPORTED_EXTENSIONS)
        }

        self.annotations = {}
        self.start_x = None
        self.start_y = None
        self.cur_rect = None
        self.selected_label = None
        self.scale = 1
        self.deletion_mode = False  # State for the new delete-by-region feature

        self.label_list, self.label_colors = self.load_label_list()

        # Layout
        self.main_frame = tk.Frame(master)
        self.main_frame.pack(fill=tk.BOTH, expand=True)
        self.canvas_frame = tk.Frame(self.main_frame)

        self.hbar = tk.Scrollbar(

        )
        self.vbar = tk.Scrollbar(
            self.canvas_frame, orient=tk.VERTICAL, command=self.canvas.yview
        )
        self.canvas.config(xscrollcommand=self.hbar.set, yscrollcommand=self.vbar.set)
        self.hbar.pack(side=tk.BOTTOM, fill=tk.X)
        self.vbar.pack(side=tk.RIGHT, fill=tk.Y)
        self.canvas.pack(side=tk.LEFT, fill=tk.BOTH, expand=True)

        # Label panel
        self.label_panel = tk.Frame(self.main_frame, padx=10, pady=10, bg="#f0f0f0")

        self.label_entry = tk.Entry(self.label_panel)
        self.label_entry.pack(pady=(10, 5))
        tk.Button(self.label_panel, text="Add Label", command=self.add_label).pack(
            pady=(0, 5)
        )

            self.label_panel, text="Delete Label", command=self.delete_label
        ).pack(pady=(0, 5))
        tk.Button(
            self.label_panel, text="Rename Label", command=self.rename_label
        ).pack(pady=(0, 5))
        tk.Button(
            self.label_panel, text="Change Color", command=self.change_label_color
        ).pack(pady=(0, 5))
        self.label_listbox.bind("<<ListboxSelect>>", self.on_label_select)

        # Navigation buttons
        btn_frame = tk.Frame(master)
        btn_frame.pack(fill=tk.X)
        tk.Button(btn_frame, text="Prev", command=self.prev_image).pack(side=tk.LEFT)
        tk.Button(btn_frame, text="Next", command=self.next_image).pack(side=tk.LEFT)
        tk.Button(
            btn_frame, text="Save Annotations", command=self.save_annotations
        ).pack(side=tk.LEFT)
        tk.Button(btn_frame, text="Split Dataset", command=self.split_dataset).pack(
            side=tk.LEFT
        )

        # Bindings
        self.canvas.bind("<ButtonPress-1>", self.on_button_press)

            (0, 0), window=self.preview_inner, anchor="nw"
        )
        self.preview_inner.bind(
            "<Configure>",
            lambda e: self.preview_canvas.config(
                scrollregion=self.preview_canvas.bbox("all")
            ),
        )

        for i in range(1, 10):
            self.master.bind(str(i), self.quick_select_label)

        self.populate_label_listbox()
        self.populate_preview_carousel()
        self.show_image()

    def enter_deletion_mode(self):
        """Activates deletion mode."""
        self.deletion_mode = True
        self.canvas.config(cursor="X_cursor")
        self.master.title(self.master.title() + " - DELETION MODE")

    def exit_special_modes(self, event=None):
        """Deactivates any special modes, like deletion mode."""
        if self.deletion_mode:
            self.deletion_mode = False
            self.canvas.config(cursor="cross")
            # Remove the mode indicator from the title
            self.master.title(self.master.title().replace(" - DELETION MODE", ""))
            if self.cur_rect:
                self.canvas.delete(self.cur_rect)
                self.cur_rect = None

    def on_button_press(self, event):
        """Start either a deletion rectangle (if in deletion_mode) or an annotation rectangle."""
        # Store canvas coordinates (always store canvas coords, convert later)
        self.start_x_canvas = self.canvas.canvasx(event.x)
        self.start_y_canvas = self.canvas.canvasy(event.y)

        # If already have a temp rect, remove it first
        if hasattr(self, "cur_rect") and self.cur_rect:
            try:
                self.canvas.delete(self.cur_rect)
            except Exception:
                pass
            self.cur_rect = None

        if self.deletion_mode:
            # draw deletion rectangle (red dashed) in canvas coordinates
            self.cur_rect = self.canvas.create_rectangle(
                self.start_x_canvas,
                self.start_y_canvas,
                self.start_x_canvas,
                self.start_y_canvas,
                outline="red",
                dash=(3, 5),
                tags="del_box",
            )
            # don't require a label for deletion mode
            return

        # Annotation mode: require a selected label
        if not self.selected_label:
            messagebox.showwarning(
                "No Label", "Please select a label before annotating."
            )
            return

        # draw annotation rectangle (blue)
        self.cur_rect = self.canvas.create_rectangle(
            self.start_x_canvas,
            self.start_y_canvas,
            self.start_x_canvas,
            self.start_y_canvas,
            outline="blue",
            tags="box",
        )

    def on_move_press(self, event):
        """Update the temporary rectangle while dragging (works for both modes)."""
        if not getattr(self, "cur_rect", None):
            return
        cur_x_canvas = self.canvas.canvasx(event.x)
        cur_y_canvas = self.canvas.canvasy(event.y)
        # update coords directly with canvas coordinates
        self.canvas.coords(
            self.cur_rect,
            self.start_x_canvas,
            self.start_y_canvas,
            cur_x_canvas,
            cur_y_canvas,
        )

    def on_button_release(self, event):
        """
        Finish deletion or annotation depending on current mode.
        Deletion removes annotations that are fully contained in the selection rectangle.
        """
        # If no temporary rect, nothing to do
        if not getattr(self, "cur_rect", None):
            # make sure to exit deletion mode gracefully if needed
            if self.deletion_mode:
                self.exit_special_modes()
            return

        # Get final canvas coords and normalize
        coords = self.canvas.coords(self.cur_rect)
        if not coords or len(coords) < 4:
            # cleanup and exit
            try:
                self.canvas.delete(self.cur_rect)
            except Exception:
                pass
            self.cur_rect = None
            if self.deletion_mode:
                self.exit_special_modes()
            return

        x1_c, y1_c, x2_c, y2_c = coords
        x1_c, x2_c = sorted([x1_c, x2_c])
        y1_c, y2_c = sorted([y1_c, y2_c])

        # --- Deletion mode ---
        if self.deletion_mode:
            # remove the temporary rect
            try:
                self.canvas.delete(self.cur_rect)
            except Exception:
                pass
            self.cur_rect = None

            # Convert to image coordinates (original image space)
            del_x1 = x1_c / self.scale
            del_y1 = y1_c / self.scale
            del_x2 = x2_c / self.scale
            del_y2 = y2_c / self.scale

            filename = self.image_ids[self.index]
            anns = self.annotations.get(filename, [])
            before_count = len(anns)

            # Keep annotations that are NOT fully contained inside deletion rect
            kept = [
                ann
                for ann in anns
                if not (
                    (ann["x1"] >= del_x1)
                    and (ann["y1"] >= del_y1)
                    and (ann["x2"] <= del_x2)
                    and (ann["y2"] <= del_y2)
                )
            ]

            removed = before_count - len(kept)
            if removed > 0:
                # update annotations and UI
                self.annotations[filename] = kept
                self.redraw_boxes()
                self.update_stats()
                print(f"[Deletion] Removed {removed} annotations from {filename}")
            else:
                print(
                    f"[Deletion] No annotations fully contained in selection for {filename}"
                )

            # exit deletion mode after one operation (keeps behaviour consistent with your UI)
            self.exit_special_modes()
            return

        # --- Annotation creation mode ---
        # remove the temporary rect (we'll redraw boxes using redraw_boxes)
        try:
            self.canvas.delete(self.cur_rect)
        except Exception:
            pass
        self.cur_rect = None

        # require label (shouldn't happen because we check at press, but double-check)
        if not self.selected_label:
            return

        # Convert canvas coords to image coords
        x1_img = int(round(x1_c / self.scale))
        y1_img = int(round(y1_c / self.scale))
        x2_img = int(round(x2_c / self.scale))
        y2_img = int(round(y2_c / self.scale))

        # clamp to image bounds (defensive)
        try:
            w, h = self.orig_img.size
        except Exception:
            w, h = None, None

        if w is not None and h is not None:
            x1_img = max(0, min(w, x1_img))
            x2_img = max(0, min(w, x2_img))
            y1_img = max(0, min(h, y1_img))
            y2_img = max(0, min(h, y2_img))

        # Discard degenerate boxes
        if x2_img <= x1_img or y2_img <= y1_img:
            return

        # Append annotation
        filename = self.image_ids[self.index]
        ann = {
            "label": self.selected_label,
            "x1": x1_img,
            "y1": y1_img,
            "x2": x2_img,
            "y2": y2_img,
        }
        self.annotations.setdefault(filename, []).append(ann)
        self.redraw_boxes()
        self.update_stats()

    # -------------------- Label Management --------------------

    def load_label_list(self):
        if os.path.exists(self.label_file):
            with open(self.label_file, "r") as f:
                data = json.load(f)
                return data.get("labels", []), data.get("colors", {})
        return [], {}

    def save_label_list(self):
        with open(self.label_file, "w") as f:
            json.dump({"labels": self.label_list, "colors": self.label_colors}, f)

    def populate_label_listbox(self):
        self.label_listbox.delete(0, tk.END)
        for i, label in enumerate(self.label_list):
            # Add a number prefix for the first 9 labels (for keyboard shortcuts 1-9)
            if i < 9:
                display_text = f"{i + 1}. {label}"
            else:
                # Add padding to align labels without a number prefix
                display_text = f"    {label}"
            self.label_listbox.insert(tk.END, display_text)

    def add_label(self):
        label = self.label_entry.get().strip()
        if label and label not in self.label_list:
            self.label_list.append(label)
            # Ask for a color
            color = colorchooser.askcolor(title=f"Choose color for {label}")[1]
            if not color:
                color = "red"
            self.label_colors[label] = color
            self.save_label_list()
            self.populate_label_listbox()
            self.label_entry.delete(0, tk.END)

    def delete_label(self):
        selection = self.label_listbox.curselection()
        if not selection:
            messagebox.showwarning("Delete Label", "Select a label to delete.")
            return

        idx = selection[0]
        label = self.label_list[idx]  # Get the clean label name from our list

        confirm = messagebox.askyesno(
            "Delete Label", f"Delete label '{label}' and remove from all annotations?"
        )
        if confirm:
            self.label_list.remove(label)
            if label in self.label_colors:
                del self.label_colors[label]
            self.save_label_list()
            self.populate_label_listbox()
            if self.selected_label == label:
                self.selected_label = None
            for fname in self.annotations:
                self.annotations[fname] = [
                    ann for ann in self.annotations[fname] if ann["label"] != label
                ]
            self.redraw_boxes()

    def rename_label(self):
        selection = self.label_listbox.curselection()
        if not selection:
            messagebox.showwarning("Rename Label", "Select a label to rename.")
            return

        idx = selection[0]
        old_label = self.label_list[idx]  # Get the clean label name

        new_label = simpledialog.askstring(
            "Rename Label", f"Enter new name for '{old_label}':", parent=self.master
        )
        if new_label and new_label.strip() and new_label != old_label:

                for txt_path in txt_paths:

                            for line in f:
                                parts = line.strip().split()
                                if len(parts) == 5:
                                    cls_id, cx, cy, bw, bh = parts
                                    cls_id = int(cls_id)
                                    cx, cy, bw, bh = map(float, (cx, cy, bw, bh))
                                    x1 = int((cx - bw / 2) * w)
                                    y1 = int((cy - bh / 2) * h)
                                    x2 = int((cx + bw / 2) * w)
                                    y2 = int((cy + bh / 2) * h)

                                        self.label_list[cls_id]
                                        if cls_id < len(self.label_list)
                                        else str(cls_id)
                                    )

                                            "x1": x1,

        for folder in [self.labels_all_dir, self.ann_json_dir]:

    def split_dataset(self):
        """Ask user for split ratio, then create YOLO dataset structure using only annotated images."""
        label_map_path = os.path.join(self.annotation_dir, "label_map.json")
        if not os.path.exists(label_map_path):
            messagebox.showwarning(
                "Split Dataset", "No annotations found. Save annotations first."
            )
            return

        # Ask user for train ratio
        ratio = simpledialog.askfloat(
            "Split Ratio", "Enter train ratio (0.0 - 1.0):", minvalue=0.0, maxvalue=1.0
        )
        if ratio is None:
            return  # User cancelled
        if not (0.0 < ratio < 1.0):
            messagebox.showwarning(
                "Invalid Ratio", "Please enter a value between 0 and 1."
            )
            return

        with open(label_map_path, "r") as f:
            label_map = json.load(f)

        # Only include images with at least one annotation
        imgs = [fname for fname, anns in self.annotations.items() if anns]

        import random

        random.seed(42)
        random.shuffle(imgs)
        n_train = int(len(imgs) * ratio)
        splits = {"train": imgs[:n_train], "val": imgs[n_train:]}

        for split_name, file_list in splits.items():
            img_out_dir = os.path.join(self.annotation_dir, "images", split_name)
            lbl_out_dir = os.path.join(self.annotation_dir, "labels", split_name)

            # ✅ Safely delete old folders even if locked or read-only
            for d in [img_out_dir, lbl_out_dir]:
                if os.path.exists(d):
                    try:
                        shutil.rmtree(d, onerror=self.remove_readonly)

                    except PermissionError as e:
                        print(f"Warning: Could not remove {d}: {e}")
                        continue  # Skip but continue creating new structure

            os.makedirs(img_out_dir, exist_ok=True)
            os.makedirs(lbl_out_dir, exist_ok=True)

            for fname in file_list:
                shutil.copy(os.path.join(self.image_dir, fname), img_out_dir)
                base, _ = os.path.splitext(fname)
                lbl_path = os.path.join(self.labels_all_dir, base + ".txt")
                if os.path.exists(lbl_path):
                    shutil.copy(lbl_path, lbl_out_dir)

        with open(os.path.join(self.annotation_dir, "data.yaml"), "w") as f:
            f.write(f"path: {os.path.abspath(self.annotation_dir)}\n")
            f.write("train: images/train\n")
            f.write("val: images/val\n")
            f.write(f"nc: {len(label_map)}\n")
            f.write("names: " + str(list(label_map.keys())) + "\n")

        messagebox.showinfo(
            "Split",
            f"Dataset split into train/val with ratio {ratio:.2f} and saved in {self.annotation_dir}",
        )

YOLO adapter using ultralytics' YOLO class. Keep this simple: load model, predict, retrain by calling ultralytics CLI.
"""
import os
import subprocess
from ultralytics import YOLO
from models.base_adapter import BaseAdapter




class YOLOAdapter(BaseAdapter):
def __init__(self, cfg, model_path=None):
super().__init__(cfg)
self.model_path = model_path or cfg.yolo_model_base
self.model = None


@property
def name(self):
return "yolov8"


def load(self):
# Load model weights into memory (fast inference)
self.model = YOLO(self.model_path)


def predict(self, image_path):
if self.model is None:
self.load()
results = self.model(image_path) # inference
out = []
for r in results:
# r.boxes possibly empty; r.boxes.data format depends on ultralytics
boxes = getattr(r, 'boxes', None)
if boxes is None:
continue
for b in boxes:
# ultralytics provides xyxy, conf, cls
xyxy = b.xyxy[0].tolist()
conf = float(b.conf[0])
cls = int(b.cls[0])
label = self.model.names.get(cls, str(cls))
x1, y1, x2, y2 = map(int, xyxy)
out.append({"label": label, "x1": x1, "y1": y1, "x2": x2, "y2": y2, "confidence": conf})
return out


def retrain(self, annotations):
"""

cmd = [
"yolo",
"task=detect",
"mode=train",
f"data={os.path.join(self.cfg.annotation_dir, 'data.yaml')}",
f"model={self.model_path}",
f"project={self.cfg.yolo_output_dir}",
"name=autotrain",
"epochs=10",
]
# This will block. Consider launching in a thread / process for non-blocking UI.
subprocess.run(cmd, check=True)
# after training, attempt to reload 'best.pt' if exists
best = os.path.join(self.cfg.yolo_output_dir, "autotrain", "weights", "best.pt")
if os.path.exists(best):
self.model_path = best
self.load()

You can implement an interactive, human-in-the-loop training loop where a base model makes predictions, a user corrects them, and those corrections are used to update the model. In practice this means: train an initial model on your data; use it to label new examples; present predictions in a GUI; let the user add missing labels or remove false positives; then incorporate those corrected examples into the training set and re-train (or fine-tune) the model. As CVAT’s documentation explains, “a small, manually labeled dataset…is used to train an initial model. Once trained, the model begins labeling new, unlabeled data. These labels are then reviewed by human annotators… The corrections made by humans are then given back to the model and…used to refine and improve it further”
cvat.ai
. Repeating this cycle gradually improves accuracy over time.

Key steps in this interactive loop are:

Initial Training: Train a model on whatever labeled data you have.

Predict & Annotate: Use the model to predict on new images/text/rows. In a GUI (see below), show these predictions (e.g. bounding boxes on images).

User Correction: The user corrects errors – draws missing boxes, erases incorrect boxes, fixes segmentation masks, corrects text labels, etc. These edits become new ground-truth labels.

Data Update: Save the corrected labels and merge them into your training set.

Retrain/Update Model: After enough new examples (the “buffer”), update the model. This can be done via incremental learning (partial updates) or by fine-tuning on the expanded dataset.

Iterate: Go back to “Predict” with the improved model and repeat.

This hybrid (automated+human) annotation process (also called active learning or incremental learning) leverages automation for routine labeling while human effort focuses on correcting mistakes
cvat.ai
. Over time, as the model improves, fewer corrections are needed and the model can label more data automatically.

Tools & Interfaces

You’ll need a labeling interface that displays model predictions and accepts user edits. Fortunately, several open-source tools and frameworks support this:

CVAT (Computer Vision Annotation Tool) – a web-based open-source tool for images/video. It lets you integrate custom models (e.g. YOLO for detection or a segmentation CNN) so that it auto-generates annotations which you then correct. For example, CVAT can wrap models (like YOLOvX or Meta’s Segment Anything Model) as plug-ins: “models (e.g., YOLOv11 or SAM2) are wrapped as Nuclio functions…once deployed, models are added to CVAT’s model registry for use in auto-annotation”
cvat.ai
. In the CVAT GUI you then review and correct these auto-annotations (bounding boxes, polygons, masks, etc.) before exporting the final labels.

Label Studio – a versatile, browser-based annotation platform supporting images, text, audio, and more. It allows you to set up tasks (e.g. bounding boxes on images, polygons, or text classification spans) with a user-friendly UI. Label Studio also has an ML backend feature: you can plug in your own model (even YOLO or a CNN) to pre-label the data, then let annotators fix it
github.com
. After corrections, you can export the updated annotations for retraining.

Doccano – an open-source text annotation tool. For NLP tasks (text classification, entity labeling, sequence labeling, etc.), Doccano provides a web UI to label text samples
github.com
. You could use it to display model-predicted labels for text and let the user adjust them.

Custom GUIs (Streamlit, Gradio, etc.) – If you need a more tailored or lightweight solution, Python frameworks like Streamlit or Gradio let you quickly build web apps. For example, you can display an image with boxes overlayed, and use drawing widgets (Streamlit’s image annotation component or Gradio’s interactive tools) to allow corrections. Similarly, for tabular data you could make a simple form to show model predictions for each row and let the user change them.

In summary, use annotation tools (CVAT, Label Studio, Doccano, etc.) for standard workflows. They support exporting in formats (e.g. COCO, YOLO, CSV) that you can feed back into training. Label Studio is advertised as “a multi-type data labeling and annotation tool” for images, text, audio, and more
github.com
. These GUIs handle the manual steps, while you handle the model training pipeline behind the scenes.

Incremental Training / Updating

The core of the system is how to update the model with new labels. Two main approaches are used:

Incremental (Online) Learning: Some algorithms support updating on-the-fly via methods like scikit-learn’s partial_fit. If your task is, say, text classification or simple regression, models like SGDClassifier, Perceptron, PassiveAggressive, or Naive Bayes can incrementally incorporate new examples without retraining from scratch. As scikit-learn docs note, “all estimators implementing the partial_fit API are candidates” for incremental learning, allowing you to feed mini-batches of new data to continually update the model
scikit-learn.org
. For example, if a user corrects the label of a sentence or adds a new data row, you could call model.partial_fit(new_features, new_labels, classes=...). This immediately updates the model weights based on just that example (or small batch). Using partial_fit avoids having to reload the entire dataset each time.

Batch Fine-Tuning: For neural networks (CNNs for images, YOLO detectors, segmentation models, etc.), you typically perform fine-tuning on the augmented dataset. That is, append the new (corrected) labeled samples to your dataset and continue training from the last checkpoint. In practice, this often means calling your training script again with the same model (loading previous weights) on the extended data. For instance, Ultralytics YOLO lets you resume training seamlessly: setting resume=True causes it to load the last .pt checkpoint (including optimizer state) and continue training
docs.ultralytics.com
. So after collecting new image annotations, you could run: model = YOLO('best.pt'); model.train(data='updated_data.yaml', epochs=10, resume=True), which fine-tunes the existing detector on the new examples. This effectively incrementally teaches the model the user’s corrections without starting from scratch. The Ultralytics docs explicitly state: “By setting resume=True, the train function will continue training from where it left off, using the state stored in the last saved model
docs.ultralytics.com
.”

For segmentation models (e.g. Mask R-CNN or U-Net), the logic is analogous: treat user-corrected masks as new ground truth, add them to your training data, and continue training. Every few corrections or epochs, you can re-evaluate the model to see improved segmentation. Even if your framework doesn’t support exact incremental updates, you can always fine-tune by training a few more epochs on the combination of old and new data.

Generic Workflow (All Data Types)

Putting it all together, a generic pipeline looks like this:

Initial Model: Train a model on your initial labeled dataset (images/text/tabular).

Automated Labeling: Use this model to predict on new unlabeled or previously labeled data.

User Review in GUI: Show the predictions to the user in a GUI (CVAT/LabelStudio for images, Doccano or custom UI for text, a simple table/UI for tabular data). The user corrects the labels (adds/removes boxes or fixes classes).

Collect Corrections: Save these corrected labels (e.g. export CSV/JSON from the tool).

Buffering: Once you have accumulated a batch of new labels (e.g. 50–100 examples or whenever convenient), proceed to update the model.

Model Update: Depending on your approach:

If using partial updates: call model.partial_fit(...) (scikit-learn) or apply an online update for each new sample
scikit-learn.org
.

If fine-tuning: combine the new examples with your existing training set and continue training (e.g. using resume=True in YOLO
docs.ultralytics.com
 or additional epochs in your DL framework).

Repeat: Use the updated model for the next round of predictions. Continue iterating this predict-review-update loop.

Over time, the model learns from the user’s corrections. The CVAT blog describes this hybrid approach: “Once trained, the model begins labeling new… data. These labels are then reviewed by human annotators… The corrections made by humans are then given back to the model… As the cycle repeats, the model becomes increasingly accurate and reliable”
cvat.ai
. This strategy works for images (detection/segmentation), text (classification/NER), and tabular data alike.

Data-Type Notes

Object Detection (YOLO, etc.): Use an annotation tool like CVAT or Label Studio to display image detections. The user can draw bounding boxes or delete wrong ones. After collecting corrected boxes (in YOLO format or COCO JSON), fine-tune your detector by continuing training. YOLO’s framework makes this easy via its resume training option
docs.ultralytics.com
.

Image Segmentation (CNN): Similar to detection, except the user edits segmentation masks (polygons or bitmasks) in the GUI. You’ll want a tool that supports mask/polygon editing (CVAT can handle masks). Then continue training your segmentation model (U-Net, Mask R-CNN, etc.) on the corrected masks. New training can incorporate these masks to improve accuracy on subtle edges.

Text Classification/NER: Use a web-based text-labeling UI (Doccano
github.com
, Label Studio, or a custom form) to show model-predicted labels on each sentence or document. The user corrects labels or entity spans. Then update your classifier (e.g. using scikit-learn’s partial_fit on the new examples
scikit-learn.org
, or fine-tune a transformer model on all data).

Tabular Data: Present data rows and the model’s prediction (class or value) in a simple GUI or spreadsheet-like interface. The user corrects any wrong labels or values. You can then call partial_fit on these rows (if using online learners) or re-run training on the growing dataset.

Throughout, try to automate as much as possible: for example, write a script that listens for completed annotation tasks (exports) and automatically triggers the retraining step when new labels are added. Many annotation platforms have APIs or command-line tools to fetch labels, so you can integrate training pipelines (for instance, CVAT has a CLI to download annotations, and Label Studio can be scripted or has a REST API).

Summary

In summary, the easiest way to build an adaptive model is via a human-in-the-loop cycle: use a model to auto-annotate, let the user correct those annotations in a GUI (such as CVAT, Label Studio, or a custom web app), and then re-train the model on the corrected data. Incremental-learning techniques (e.g. scikit-learn’s partial_fit
scikit-learn.org
